title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study that isolates downstream validator and bounded repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Using a 1,000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2,000 paired episodes) and a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), we compared a baseline single‑shot LLM generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (single allowed repair + canary semantics). The declared model/provider was gpt‑5‑mini (openai_responses); execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). With exactly one sampled initial generation reused by both arms per pair, differences can arise only from deterministic validation and permitted repairs. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] (descriptive). Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred; total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar as the confirmatory outcome, explicitly label the one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, a near‑unity baseline, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation promises operational gains but creates safety risks: ordering errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can make plausible command sequences harmful. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination and structured‑output failures that materially affect correctness in code and configuration generation, motivating pipeline architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This work asks a tightly specified question under preregistration: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (preregistered generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), to what degree can a deterministic downstream validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes relative to reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions so that any paired difference is attributable only to deterministic validation and the permitted repair.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) using a deterministic selection rule from a synthetic challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full artifact‑grounded reporting of execution accounting and the preregistered confirmatory result (exact two‑sided McNemar, p = 0.0625). (3) A concise, evidence‑grounded interpretation clarifying why descriptive bootstrap summaries may diverge from the preregistered confirmatory test in the sparse‑discordance regime and what follow‑ups are needed.
sections.related_work:
LLM behavior for structured outputs shows frequent prompt sensitivity and hallucination that can produce incorrect or non‑executable artifacts; empirical surveys and controlled studies in code and configuration tasks document these failure modes and motivate verifier‑assisted pipelines [1],[2]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning have been shown to reduce syntactic and executability errors in structured domains, though much of that evidence arises outside NetOps and transfer depends on validator fidelity and tooling [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers propose verifier‑assisted repair, digital‑twin validation, and governance/proof‑carrying mechanisms to mitigate automation risks; these works present prototypes and architectural evaluations that stress the dependence of operational reliability on validator coverage and external protocol enforcement [4],[5],[6].

Our experiment complements these lines by preregistering a paired estimand that isolates downstream verification and repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics; this avoids conflating downstream interventions with first‑pass prompt or decoding differences and clarifies the scope of what the paired comparison measures.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen prior to any hosted‑model calls (preregistration_sha256 recorded in the execution manifest = ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Key preregistered elements: paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministically drawn from challenging_workflow_stress_v1; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (single sampled initial generation per task deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as a descriptive statistic.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial candidate per task was deterministically reused for baseline and guarded episodes; the guarded pipeline could then (a) accept that candidate, (b) reject it and invoke at most one permitted repair call, and (c) accept or reject the repair result. Therefore, any paired outcome difference arises solely from deterministic validator decisions and the permitted repair. The design does not measure effects of independent first‑pass generation, constrained decoding, or alternate prompt templates that were not executed.

Model and runtime configuration. The declared model/provider in the archived model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The orchestration adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation employed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0). The validator enforces task manifest constraints (required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, protected interfaces) deterministically via a digital‑twin emulator and returns a binary safe‑deploy verdict.

Execution accounting and missingness plan. The preregistered sampling and retry policy specified maximum_model_calls = 2000 (planned episodes = 2000) and maximum_attempts_per_call = 1. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 2000, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 1005, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}. The preregistered primary analysis uses complete_pair_primary handling of missingness; sensitivity analyses treating failed episodes as unsafe were preregistered but not required because no failed episodes occurred.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run executed per preregistration: planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; complete_pairs = 1000; failed episodes = 0. Provider audit records hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair calls = 5). All deterministic reconciliation checks passed and contamination checks found no prompt leakage.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The 2×2 paired contingency table (archived as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; this does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold, so the preregistered H1 is not supported.

Bootstrap summary and why it can diverge from the exact test. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]. This paired bootstrap was specified as a descriptive summary; with extremely sparse discordant counts (here n10 + n01 = 5) bootstrap resampling of pairs can produce resamples whose percentile bounds exclude zero even when an exact test is not significant. The bootstrap interval is therefore sensitive to the discrete resampling distribution in the sparse‑discordance regime and cannot be used to overturn the preregistered exact McNemar confirmatory outcome. We report the bootstrap interval as preregistered and label any one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc because a one‑sided test was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and power mismatch. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline ≈ 0.60 with a target absolute effect of 0.15 to obtain >80% power. The observed baseline success (0.995) is far higher than assumed; near‑unity baseline rates produce very few discordant pairs and thereby reduce sensitivity of the exact paired test to detect small absolute gains. Consequently, the non‑significant two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625) should be interpreted in context: it is the preregistered confirmatory outcome, but the design in this observed regime has limited power to detect small absolute improvements.

Mechanistic scope under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because initial candidates were held identical across arms, only deterministic validator decisions and the permitted single repair call could create paired differences. The five observed repairs illustrate that validators with adequate rule coverage can correct certain sequence or protected‑field violations; however, the small number of repairs limits inference about repair efficacy across diverse failure modes. Measuring effects of prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or larger repair budgets requires follow‑ups that intentionally vary generation semantics or repair allowance, which were not part of the frozen preregistration.

Threats to validity. Construct validity depends on validator rule coverage: omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistered deterministic seeding and zero failed episodes, but the shared_initial_candidate design intentionally excludes first‑pass generation variance. External validity is limited by a single model (gpt‑5‑mini), a synthetic task corpus, and a deterministic digital‑twin validator; heterogeneity across device vendors and production artifacts remains to be tested. Conclusion validity is limited by sparse discordant counts and the resulting discrete test behavior.

Recommended preregistered follow‑ups (artifact‑grounded). The archived artifacts permit and motivate these preregistered extensions: (1) relax shared_initial_candidate semantics to run independent generation arms and measure prompt/decoding effects; (2) sweep repair budgets (0..k) to estimate marginal returns per failure class; (3) expand validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity; and (4) evaluate multiple model families to map model dependence. Each follow‑up should include power calculations aligned to plausible baseline failure rates.
sections.conclusion:
In a preregistered paired study on a 1,000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005. The preregistered exact McNemar result is the confirmatory inference; paired bootstrap summaries and an exploratory one‑sided McNemar are reported but explicitly labeled as descriptive/exploratory. These artifact‑grounded results show that downstream verifier/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflows, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator coverage, and repair budget. Full preregistration, execution manifests, raw outputs, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run to enable reproducible, preregistered follow‑ups.

Orchestration and validator: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0). Preregistration: cand‑003‑stud‑001 (frozen prior to any model calls; preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest = ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Immutable initial master prompt reference archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. After the autonomy lock, literature review, preregistration finalization, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and automated revisions were performed by the autonomous research run; no human manually edited the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Single‑model scope: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and target effect = 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains with the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
